report_title: Sea Turtle (Teal Kurma / Marbled Dust / SILICON / Cosmic Wolf / UNC1326) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: Cisco Talos 'DNS Hijacking Abuses Trust in Core Internet Service' and 'Sea Turtle keeps its head above water' (2019, https://blog.talosintelligence.com/seaturtle/); Hunt & Hackett 'Turkish espionage campaigns in the Netherlands' (2024-01-05, https://www.huntandhackett.com/blog/turkish-espionage-campaigns) and threat-actor profile (https://www.huntandhackett.com/threats/actors/seaturtle); MITRE ATT&CK Group Sea Turtle G1041 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1041/) and Software SnappyTCP S1163 (https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1163/); PwC 'The Tortoise and The Malwahare' (2023); Microsoft Marbled Dust reporting

actor.name: Sea Turtle
related_clusters: DNSpionage (overlapping/adjacent DNS-hijacking activity, Iran-nexus — distinct actor, distinguished by Talos)
SnappyTCP (custom Linux/Unix reverse-shell webshell, MITRE S1163)
actor.attribution: Turkey-nexus, assessed to be a state-aligned espionage actor operating in support of Turkish state interests. Attribution to a Türkiye-linked actor is supported by convergence across multiple independent vendors (Cisco Talos, Hunt & Hackett, PwC, Microsoft) on victimology (Kurdish/PKK-affiliated groups, Cypriot and Greek government/telecom, Middle East and North Africa government and telecom), operational tempo aligned to Turkish geopolitical interest, and consistent DNS-hijacking tradecraft. No public sanction or indictment names a specific Turkish state entity; attribution is analytic, not adjudicated. Assessed at medium-high confidence — strong tradecraft/victimology convergence but limited primary-source confirmation of state direction.
targeted_regions_mena: Middle East and North Africa (government, telecom, DNS registries)
targeted_sectors: IT service providers / managed service providers

key_campaigns.name: DNS hijacking of core internet services (Talos)
key_campaigns.summary: Signature campaign: rather than compromising ultimate victims directly, Sea Turtle compromised third-party DNS registrars, registries and DNS providers, then altered NS and A records for targeted organizations to redirect victim traffic to actor-controlled man-in-the-middle (MitM) nodes hosted on VPS infrastructure. The MitM nodes presented CA-signed X.509 certificates (Let's Encrypt, Comodo/Sectigo) or self-signed certs to defeat browser warnings and intercepted credentials for VPNs, webmail and other login portals. Actors set very low DNS TTLs (as low as 1 second) to minimize caching and quickly revert records. Initial access to the intermediary providers used exploitation of known CVEs on internet-facing systems.

key_campaigns.name: Turkish espionage campaigns in the Netherlands (Hunt & Hackett)
key_campaigns.summary: Espionage operations against Dutch and European telecom, media, ISP and IT firms, and against Kurdish (PKK-affiliated) websites. Initial access in a 2023 case used a compromised-but-legitimate cPanel account. Actors deployed the custom SnappyTCP Linux/Unix reverse-shell webshell for persistence and C2 (two variants: OpenSSL/TLS-encrypted and cleartext), used a modified Socat for tunnelling, installed the Adminer database tool in public web directories, harvested and tar-archived email archives into internet-accessible web directories for retrieval, and performed anti-forensics (unsetting Bash and MySQL history, overwriting Linux system logs).

malware: SnappyTCP (custom Linux/Unix reverse-shell webshell, MITRE S1163)
tooling_observed: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
Socat (modified, used as tunnelling / C2 relay)
Adminer (web database management tool, staged in public web dirs)
NoHup (keep SnappyTCP running after session close)
Let's Encrypt / Comodo / Sectigo / self-signed X.509 certificates

ttps.procedure_description: Actors map the DNS architecture of targets and their upstream registrars/registries/DNS providers to identify which third-party DNS operator to compromise in order to hijack resolution for the ultimate victim.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — reconnaissance of public DNS records occurs off-victim against public infrastructure and is not endpoint-observable; hunt/intel candidate via external attack-surface and DNS-footprint monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Actors select deliberate victims aligned to Turkish state interest (Kurdish/PKK-affiliated organizations, Cypriot/Greek and MENA government and telecom), indicating targeted organizational research rather than opportunistic scanning.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — organizational targeting research is off-victim; intel candidate only

ttps.procedure_description: Actors stood up actor-controlled nameservers (ns1/ns2.intersecdns.com and ns1/ns2.lcjcomputing.com, resolving to 95.179.150.101) to serve falsified DNS responses to victim queries after hijacking records.
observed_tooling: malicious/actor-controlled nameservers (intersecdns.com, lcjcomputing.com)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — adversary-operated nameservers are off-victim infrastructure; hunt/intel candidate via passive-DNS and infrastructure tracking of the named nameserver domains/IP

ttps.procedure_description: Actors rented a large set of VPS instances (26 documented MitM IPs across multiple hosting providers and regions) to host man-in-the-middle nodes that impersonate legitimate victim services.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — VPS acquisition is off-victim; intel candidate via tracking the documented MitM IP set in passive DNS / netflow at the perimeter

ttps.procedure_description: Actors register domains used for nameserver and C2 infrastructure (e.g. intersecdns.com, lcjcomputing.com, boord.info, systemctl.network) to blend with legitimate DNS/service naming.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — domain registration is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via WHOIS/registration and certificate-transparency monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: Actors obtained CA-signed X.509 certificates (Let's Encrypt, Comodo/Sectigo) — and used self-signed certs — for victim domains so the MitM node presents a trusted certificate and avoids browser TLS warnings during credential interception.
observed_tooling: Let's Encrypt / Comodo / Sectigo / self-signed X.509 certificates
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — certificate acquisition happens at third-party CAs; hunt candidate via Certificate Transparency log monitoring for unexpected certs issued for owned domains

ttps.procedure_description: Actors install the obtained/forged certificates on the MitM VPS nodes so that intercepted TLS sessions to spoofed login portals appear valid to victims.
observed_tooling: Let's Encrypt / Comodo / Sectigo / self-signed X.509 certificates
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — certificate installation on off-victim MitM infrastructure is not visible to the victim; hunt via CT-log correlation and TLS-fingerprint anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: Actors obtain and operationalize public tooling — a modified Socat for tunnelling, the Adminer web DB tool, and SnappyTCP (based on a since-removed public GitHub project).
observed_tooling: Socat (modified, used as tunnelling / C2 relay)
Adminer (web database management tool, staged in public web dirs)
SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition is off-endpoint; downstream on-host use of each tool is where detection lands — intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: Signature tradecraft: rather than attacking the ultimate victim directly, actors compromise third-party DNS registrars, ccTLD registries and DNS providers, then alter the victim's NS and A records at the compromised operator to redirect resolution to actor-controlled MitM nodes. TTL is frequently lowered to as little as 1 second to limit caching and allow rapid record reversion.
observed_tooling: malicious/actor-controlled nameservers (intersecdns.com, lcjcomputing.com)
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the record tampering happens at the registrar/registry/provider (off the victim's own systems); hunt-leaning via registry-lock monitoring, DNS-record change alerting, passive-DNS anomaly detection, DNSSEC validation failures and Certificate-Transparency monitoring rather than host telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Primary initial-access vector against intermediary providers and victims: exploitation of known CVEs on internet-facing systems — Cisco ASA directory traversal (CVE-2018-0296), Cisco IOS/switch and ISR RCEs (CVE-2017-3881, CVE-2017-6736), Apache Tomcat RCE (CVE-2017-12617), Drupalgeddon2 (CVE-2018-7600), phpMyAdmin PHP injection (CVE-2009-1151) and Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271). Consistent with reporting on Citrix/NetScaler and webmail/VPN RCE exploitation.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — exploitation of these specific CVEs on internet-facing appliances/servers is the strongest detection surface: WAF/appliance/web-server logs, exploit signatures, anomalous requests to vulnerable endpoints, post-exploit process/file activity and version/patch-state monitoring all apply

ttps.procedure_description: Actors abuse internet-facing remote services for access, including SSH logons originating from commercial VPN providers and reuse of hosting/cPanel access to reach victim webservers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — anomalous SSH/remote-service logons (VPN-provider source IPs, new geolocation, off-hours) are detectable via authentication logs and identity analytics, but blend with legitimate remote administration

ttps.procedure_description: By compromising DNS providers, registrars, registries and IT/telecom service providers, actors abuse the trust those intermediaries hold to reach downstream ultimate victims (supply-chain / trusted-relationship access).
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the compromise occurs at a trusted third party outside the victim's boundary; hunt/intel candidate via third-party-risk monitoring and provider-side change alerting

ttps.procedure_description: Actors use valid credentials — including a compromised-but-legitimate cPanel hosting account (2023 case) and credentials harvested via DNS-hijack MitM interception — to authenticate to victim systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — authentication with valid stolen credentials is detectable via anomalous-logon analytics (new source, impossible travel, first-seen device) but overlaps with legitimate use

ttps.procedure_description: Signature credential-access behavior: after DNS records are hijacked, victim traffic is transparently proxied through actor-controlled MitM nodes presenting valid TLS certificates. The nodes impersonate VPN concentrators, webmail and other login portals to capture submitted usernames and passwords before relaying traffic onward.
observed_tooling: Let's Encrypt / Comodo / Sectigo / self-signed X.509 certificates
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the interception happens on off-victim MitM infrastructure between the client and the real service; hunt-leaning via certificate-transparency monitoring, TLS certificate/issuer changes for owned services, unexpected resolution IPs and DNSSEC-validation failures rather than endpoint telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Actors interpose spoofed login portals (served from MitM nodes) into the authentication flow of legitimate victim services, harvesting credentials as users authenticate to what appears to be the genuine portal.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — the spoofed authentication flow lives on off-victim infrastructure; hunt candidate via user reports, TLS/issuer anomalies and impossible-travel authentication signals downstream

ttps.procedure_description: Actors leverage exploitation of vulnerable server/appliance software (the CVEs above) to achieve code execution on internet-facing intermediary and victim systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — exploitation-driven execution is detectable via crash/anomaly telemetry and unexpected child processes spawned by server/appliance software, but requires instrumentation on the exploited host

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
ttps.procedure_description: Actors execute commands via the Unix/Bash shell on compromised Linux/Unix webservers to deploy SnappyTCP, run Socat, stage tools and copy/collect data.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
Socat (modified, used as tunnelling / C2 relay)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — shell command execution on Unix webservers is observable via auditd/EDR process telemetry; webserver processes (e.g. apache/php) spawning bash/socat/nohup children are high-fidelity indicators

ttps.procedure_description: Actors deploy the custom SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (MITRE S1163) into web-accessible directories on Linux/Unix victim servers for persistence and basic C2. Two variants exist: one uses OpenSSL to create a TLS-secured channel, the other sends requests in cleartext. On start it reads a config file with a C2 domain and port and issues an HTTP GET for the URI 'sy.php'; it acts on the response only if the server returns header 'X-Auth-43245-S-20' and the body is of sufficient size and does not begin with '@'.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — the SnappyTCP webshell is a crisp endpoint detection: new/unexpected executables or scripts in web roots, the 'sy.php' request URI and 'X-Auth-43245-S-20' header, and webserver-user processes making outbound connections are all actor-specific, high-fidelity signals

ttps.procedure_description: Actors launch SnappyTCP with NoHup so the reverse shell keeps running after the initiating SSH/web session closes, detaching it from session hang-up signals.
observed_tooling: NoHup (keep SnappyTCP running after session close)
SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — nohup invocations wrapping network binaries (e.g. nohup ./snappytcp / nohup socat) are detectable via process-execution command-line telemetry on the host, but nohup is also used legitimately

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
ttps.procedure_description: SnappyTCP is delivered/handled as source and compiled on the victim host (the OpenSSL-linked and cleartext variants are built locally), reducing static-detection surface for the delivered payload.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — on-host compilation (gcc/cc invocations, especially by web/service users linking against OpenSSL) is detectable via process-execution telemetry but requires baselining on servers where compilers are legitimately present

ttps.technique_name: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
ttps.procedure_description: Following SSH sessions, actors overwrite/clear Linux system logs under /var/log as an anti-forensic measure to remove evidence of their activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — truncation/overwriting of /var/log files is detectable via file-integrity monitoring, auditd watches on log paths, and log-volume/continuity gaps forwarded off-host before tampering

ttps.procedure_description: Actors unset/clear the Bash command-history file and the MySQL history file to prevent their commands from being recorded during interactive sessions.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — unset HISTFILE / HISTFILESIZE=0 / removal of ~/.bash_history and ~/.mysql_history are detectable via process command-line and file-deletion auditing when host logging is forwarded off-box

ttps.procedure_description: Actors reuse compromised local accounts (e.g. the hijacked cPanel hosting account) to maintain access to victim webservers across sessions.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — reuse of local hosting/webserver accounts is detectable via authentication analytics (new source IP from VPN providers, off-hours logons) but overlaps with legitimate administration

ttps.procedure_description: Actors install the Adminer web-based database management tool in public web directories to browse and extract data from victim MySQL/other databases.
observed_tooling: Adminer (web database management tool, staged in public web dirs)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — presence of Adminer (or similar db-admin PHP tools) in web roots and anomalous database queries from the webserver are detectable via file-integrity monitoring and DB query auditing, but require web/DB-tier visibility

ttps.procedure_description: Actors collect victim e-mail archives from the compromised mail/web host — a primary espionage objective — copying the mailbox archive for staging and retrieval.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — access to and copying of local mailbox/archive files by non-mail-service processes is detectable via file-access auditing on the mail host, but needs mailbox-path instrumentation

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: Actors use tar to compress collected e-mail archives prior to exfiltration.
observed_tooling: tar (archive email data)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tar/gzip execution producing large archives of mailbox/data directories, especially by web/service accounts, is detectable via process command-line and file-write telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: Actors copy the tar'd e-mail archive into the public web directory of the compromised website so it is directly reachable from the internet for later retrieval.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — appearance of large archive files (e.g. .tar/.tar.gz) inside internet-facing web roots is a strong, specific detection via file-integrity monitoring and web-root content baselining

ttps.procedure_description: Actors collect files and data of interest from the local compromised system in support of espionage objectives.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — local data collection is common; suspicious mainly via staging patterns (into web roots) and process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: SnappyTCP communicates over HTTP: on startup it issues an HTTP GET for URI 'sy.php' to its configured C2 and keys off the response header 'X-Auth-43245-S-20'; channels are established to C2 domains over port 443.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — outbound HTTP GETs to '/sy.php' and the distinctive 'X-Auth-43245-S-20' header from a webserver host are actor-specific network detections via proxy/IDS and host netflow

ttps.procedure_description: One SnappyTCP variant uses OpenSSL to wrap its C2 channel in TLS, encrypting the reverse-shell traffic (over port 443) to blend with normal HTTPS and defeat inspection.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — TLS-wrapped C2 blends with normal HTTPS; detectable via JA3/JA4 TLS-fingerprint anomalies, connections to the documented C2 domains/IPs, and a webserver process opening outbound 443 to non-CDN hosts

ttps.procedure_description: Actors use a modified Socat (retrieved from actor infrastructure at 193.34.167.245/c00n/socat) to relay/tunnel connections and proxy C2, obscuring the true source of traffic.
observed_tooling: Socat (modified, used as tunnelling / C2 relay)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — socat execution and the resulting relay connections are detectable via process command-line and network telemetry on the host, though socat is also a legitimate admin tool

ttps.procedure_description: Actors exfiltrate the staged e-mail archive by downloading it directly over HTTP/HTTPS from the internet-accessible public web directory of the compromised host (web-accessible file retrieval).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — large outbound web downloads of archive files from web roots to non-victim client IPs are detectable via webserver access logs and egress monitoring, but require web-tier log correlation

ttps.procedure_description: Actors can also move collected data out over the SnappyTCP/Socat C2 channel established to their infrastructure.
observed_tooling: SnappyTCP reverse-shell webshell (TLS/OpenSSL and cleartext variants)
Socat (modified, used as tunnelling / C2 relay)
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — data egress riding the C2 channel is detectable via volumetric/beaconing anomalies from a webserver host to the documented C2 endpoints, but is masked when TLS-wrapped

detection_signals: Unexpected changes to your organization's authoritative NS and A records at the registrar/registry/DNS provider, especially abrupt TTL reductions toward 1 second — monitor via registry-lock alerts, DNS-record change monitoring and passive DNS

New / unexpected TLS certificates issued for your owned domains (Let's Encrypt, Comodo/Sectigo) surfacing in Certificate Transparency logs, or issuer/serial changes on portals — indicates possible MitM staging
Client resolution of your services to unexpected IPs (compare against the documented MitM VPS IP set) and DNSSEC-validation failures
SnappyTCP webshell on Linux/Unix web hosts: new/unexpected executables or scripts in web roots; webserver user (apache/www-data/php) spawning bash, socat or nohup child processes
Outbound HTTP GET to request URI '/sy.php' and the distinctive response header 'X-Auth-43245-S-20'; webserver host opening outbound connections on port 443 to non-CDN hosts / documented C2 domains
On-host compilation of a network binary linking OpenSSL by a web/service account (gcc/cc invocations building the SnappyTCP TLS variant)
nohup wrapping a network binary (nohup ./snappytcp, nohup socat) to survive session close
Retrieval of a modified socat from http://193.34.167.245/c00n/socat and subsequent socat relay/tunnel connections
Adminer (or similar db-admin PHP) appearing in public web directories and anomalous DB queries from the webserver
Large tar/tar.gz archives of mailbox/e-mail data appearing inside internet-facing web roots, followed by external HTTP(S) downloads of those files
Anti-forensics on Linux hosts: overwriting/truncation of /var/log files, unset HISTFILE / removal of ~/.bash_history and MySQL history immediately after SSH sessions

Exploitation attempts and post-exploit activity against internet-facing Cisco ASA/IOS/ISR, Apache Tomcat, Drupal, phpMyAdmin and Bash (CVE-2018-0296, CVE-2017-3881, CVE-2017-6736, CVE-2017-12617, CVE-2018-7600, CVE-2009-1151, CVE-2014-6271) — appliance/web-server logs and version/patch-state monitoring
SSH logons to hosting/cPanel and webservers originating from commercial VPN provider IP ranges (e.g. M247, Arelion, Snel.com) or the documented actor IPs

Traffic to/from documented C2 and MitM infrastructure: 82.102.19.88, 62.115.255.163, 193.34.167.245, 93.115.22.212, 95.179.176.250, 95.179.150.101, and the 26 Talos MitM VPS IPs; domains forward.boord.info, lo0.systemctl.network, and the intersecdns.com / lcjcomputing.com nameservers
notes: Primary sources: Cisco Talos Sea Turtle reporting (2019) for the DNS-hijacking campaign, exploited CVEs, MitM/nameserver infrastructure and the 26 MitM VPS IPs; Hunt & Hackett 'Turkish espionage campaigns in the Netherlands' (2024-01-05) for SnappyTCP, Socat, Adminer, anti-forensics, email-archive collection/staging and the Netherlands C2/VPN IOCs; enriched with MITRE ATT&CK Group Sea Turtle G1041 and Software SnappyTCP S1163, and PwC/Microsoft (Marbled Dust) corroboration. Overall confidence is high for the technical TTPs/IOCs (multiple independent primary vendor reports with IOC appendices); attribution to a Türkiye-nexus state-aligned actor is medium-high (strong victimology/tradecraft convergence, no public indictment naming a state entity) and is reflected in actor.attribution_confidence. actor.mitre_id intentionally left empty per tasking; the public MITRE group id G1041 is cited only in source/aliases/notes, never as the actor id. ATT&CK normalization for THIS environment's bundled (reorganized) dataset: Defense-Evasion techniques use tactic slug 'stealth'; anti-forensic log/history clearing uses the 'defense-impairment' family — Clear Linux/Mac System Logs = T1685.006 and Prevent Command History Logging = T1690 (both validated present in attack_dump.json). Every technique_id in this pack was validated as a key in attack_dump.json (697 techniques) before inclusion — zero invalid IDs. DETECTION-CANDIDATE (medium/high feasibility, on-host/appliance): T1190 CVE exploitation, T1505.003 SnappyTCP webshell, T1059.004 Unix-shell child processes, T1071.001 sy.php + X-Auth-43245-S-20 C2, T1074.002 archives in web roots, T1685.006/T1690 anti-forensics, T1560.001 tar, T1213.006 Adminer, T1114.001 email collection, T1090 socat, T1078/T1133 anomalous SSH/cPanel logons. HUNT-LEANING (low feasibility, off-victim/infrastructure/DNS): T1584.002 DNS-server compromise & record tampering (observed at registrar/resolver, not on the victim), T1557/T1556 MitM credential interception on off-victim nodes, T1588.004/T1608.003 certificate acquisition/staging (Certificate-Transparency hunt), T1583.001/.002/.003 adversary infrastructure, T1590.002/T1591 reconnaissance, T1199 trusted-relationship compromise — these route to threat-hunting via DNS-change monitoring, passive DNS, DNSSEC and CT-log analysis rather than detection engineering. IOC handling: all indicators are taken verbatim from the Talos and Hunt & Hackett appendices/blog bodies; defang brackets removed for raw machine-readable values per spec; legitimate/hosting-provider ASNs (M247, Arelion, Snel.com) named only as context in detection_signals, not as IOCs. NO file hashes are included: the only sample hash surfaced (a SnappyTCP-related modified-Socat SHA-1) was returned truncated to 39 hex characters and could not be validated to a full 40-char SHA-1, so it was intentionally omitted rather than risk a malformed indicator — ingest the Hunt & Hackett report's original IOC table directly if the sample hash is required downstream.
